meaning: This first branch asks what a Bitcoin transaction is before any of its bytes are read
analogy: A transaction is a signed letter asking every ledger to update itself.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group collects the three ideas a reader needs before the bytes make sense: the transaction itself, the ownership record that it asks full nodes to change, and the parts that every transaction is built from
analogy: a signed letter that asks every ledger to change
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel TransactionIdea

meaning: A transaction is the data Alice uses to convince every full node to update its database so that some bitcoins she controls are recorded as controlled by Bob.
analogy: a signed letter asking every bank branch to update its ledger.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: The ownership record of a full node
meaning: Every full node keeps its own copy of the database that says which bitcoins are controlled by whom, and a transaction is accepted when the node agrees to update that copy.
analogy: a land register that every town keeps an identical copy of.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A serialized transaction has a version, an inputs field, an outputs field, a lock time and, when it spends segwit outputs, a marker, a flag and a witness structure.
analogy: a cheque with boxes for payer, payee, amount and signature.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Serialization is the writing of a data structure as a sequence of bytes so that it can be stored, hashed or sent
analogy: packing a letter flat for the post
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel SerializationFormats

meaning: A serialized transaction is the transaction written as the sequence of bytes that Bitcoin Core hashes, relays and stores; the book prints Alice's as 388 hexadecimal characters.
analogy: a letter flattened into one long strip of tape.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The extended serialization format of BIP144 adds a marker byte, a flag byte and a witness structure to the legacy layout, for transactions that spend segwit outputs.
analogy: the same letter with a signed slip tucked in at the end.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Legacy serialization is the original transaction format, without the marker, flag and witness structure; it is still used for every transaction that spends no witness program.
analogy: the plain letter, before the extra slip was invented.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The partially signed bitcoin transaction (PSBT) format of BIPs 174 and 370 lets an untrusted program build a transaction template that trusted programs holding the keys verify and complete.
analogy: a form passed round the office until every signer has signed.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A byte map draws a serialized transaction with each field at its byte position and length, so that the hexadecimal can be read as named parts.
analogy: a floor plan showing which room each byte lives in.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch reads the first six bytes of Alice's transaction: the four-byte version and, because her transaction carries a witness, the marker and the flag that announce the extended format
analogy: Version, marker and flag are the edition number and labels on the envelope.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The version field is the four-byte little-endian integer at the start of every transaction
analogy: the edition number printed on a form
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel VersionField

meaning: Version 1 is the original transaction version, written 01000000 in little-endian order; every transaction must follow its rules, and Alice's transaction uses it.
analogy: edition 1 of a form, still valid in every office.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Version 2 transactions were introduced by the BIP68 soft fork; only in a transaction of version 2 or higher is a sequence value below 2 to the 31 a relative timelock, and BIP112's opcode fails below version 2.
analogy: edition 2, which adds a waiting-period box to the form.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The version 3 proposal, BIP431, changes only the relay policy of full nodes: a version 3 transaction accepts topological restrictions in exchange for protection against pinning attacks; Bitcoin Core treats it as standard since release 28.0.
analogy: a draft edition that offices may choose to accept.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A presigned transaction is signed but not broadcast, perhaps for years; a later rule that applies to its version could make it permanently invalid, so new constraints are reserved for new version numbers.
analogy: a post-dated cheque kept in a drawer.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The marker and the flag are the two bytes that follow the version in the extended serialization format
analogy: a fragile label on a parcel
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel MarkerAndFlag

meaning: The marker is the byte 0x00 after the version of an extended-format transaction; a legacy parser would read it as a count of zero inputs, which no transaction can have, so it signals the extended format.
analogy: a sticker on a parcel saying special contents inside.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The flag is the byte after the marker; it is 0x01 in the current protocol, other values are reserved for upgrades, and BIP144 reads it as a bit vector for adding non-committed data later.
analogy: a second sticker that names the kind of extras.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch reads the inputs field of a transaction, the 42 bytes of Alice's transaction that say where the bitcoins she spends come from
analogy: Inputs are the banknotes you hand over, each named by its address.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The input list is the inputs field as a whole: a count followed by that many inputs
analogy: a receipt listing the notes you hand over
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel InputList

meaning: The input count is the compactSize integer that opens the inputs field; it must be at least one, and transaction size limits keep it to a few thousand in practice.
analogy: counting how many cheques are stapled to a payment.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A compactSize unsigned integer is one byte for values up to 252 and otherwise a prefix byte 0xfd, 0xfe or 0xff followed by the value as a 2-, 4- or 8-byte little-endian integer.
analogy: a ticket machine: small numbers get short tickets.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual CompactSize; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin programs use several variable-length integers: compactSize in transactions and the P2P protocol, Bitcoin Core's VarInts in its UTXO database, and the unrelated Compact encoding of a block header's nBits field.
analogy: three kinds of ticket sold under one name.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The outpoint is the field with which an input points at the previous output it spends
analogy: a street address with building and flat
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel OutpointField

meaning: An outpoint is the 32-byte txid of a previous transaction followed by the 4-byte index of one of its outputs; every input has exactly one, and a node uses it to find the output being spent.
analogy: a street address: building number plus flat number.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The txid in an outpoint is the 32-byte double-SHA-256 identifier of the transaction that created the output being spent, stored in internal byte order.
analogy: the building number in that address.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The output index is the 4-byte unsigned integer after the txid in an outpoint; it chooses one output of the previous transaction, counting from zero.
analogy: the flat number inside the building, counted from zero.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: One of Bitcoin's consensus rules forbids any output from being spent more than once within a valid blockchain: Alice cannot use the same previous output to pay both Bob and Carol.
analogy: a banknote that can be handed over only once.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Two transactions that each try to spend the same previous output are conflicting transactions; only one of them can be included in a valid blockchain.
analogy: two cheques written against the same banknote.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin Core keeps a database of every unspent transaction output with essential metadata; each new block removes the outputs its transactions spend and adds the outputs they create.
analogy: a drawer holding only the banknotes nobody has spent.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group explains the book's sidebar on the two byte orders of a hash
analogy: a book you can read from the front or the back
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel ByteOrder

meaning: A digest is the output of a hash function; Bitcoin uses digests as identifiers of blocks and transactions, in commitments, and in proof of work.
analogy: a fingerprint taken from a whole document.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual Digest; lab example

meaning: Internal byte order is the order in which a digest's bytes appear within transactions and blocks and are fed to hash functions; the book also calls it little-endian.
analogy: reading a phone number from its last digit.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Display byte order is the reversed form in which identifiers are shown to users and accepted by explorers and bitcoin-cli; the book also calls it big-endian.
analogy: reading the phone number the usual way round.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The input script is the second field of every input, after the outpoint and before the sequence, and it is length-prefixed
analogy: a keyhole that legacy inputs fill with the key
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel InputScriptField

meaning: The input script is the legacy field in which a spending transaction places its signatures and other authorising data; a segwit input leaves it empty.
analogy: the key you hand over at the door.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The length prefix is the compactSize integer before an input script that says how many bytes of script follow; it is 0x6b for the book's 107-byte example and 0x00 for Alice's empty script.
analogy: a label on a box saying how many items it holds.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch reads the last four bytes of an input, which the book calls its sequence number, and follows the three meanings the field has carried
analogy: The sequence field is a booth ticket whose meaning changed three times.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The original sequence-based replacement is the first meaning of the field: the book says the sequence field was originally intended to allow creation of multiple versions of the same transaction, with later versions replacing earlier versions as candidates for confirmation, the sequence number tracking the version of the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
analogy: an order slip you can reissue until the kitchen closes
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel SequenceReplacement

meaning: The sequence is the 4-byte field that ends every input; its maximal value 0xffffffff, called final, opts out of replacement, of the BIP125 signal and of any relative timelock.
analogy: a counter on a ticket that the booth can reissue.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The setup transaction deposits Alice's and Bob's money into a multisignature output that needs both signatures; the refund transaction, with sequence 0, pays each their deposit back and is kept unbroadcast.
analogy: a locked deposit box that needs two keys.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A payment channel is a protocol in which two parties sign many versions of one transaction off the chain, each with a higher sequence, and broadcast only the final one; the book's card game is the original form.
analogy: a bar tab: many orders, one bill at the end.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Unlimited free replacement let an attacker with 1,000 replacements a minute at 200 bytes each cost 50,000 relaying nodes about 10 GB of bandwidth a minute for 20 KB of their own, so the scheme was disabled.
analogy: refiling the same form again and again to clog the office.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Replace-by-fee is the second meaning of the sequence field
analogy: outbidding someone at an auction
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel ReplaceByFee

meaning: Opt-in replace-by-fee is the relay policy under which a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate replaces an unconfirmed one that signalled replaceability; the replacement must also pay for its own relay.
analogy: outbidding someone at an auction
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: By BIP125 an unconfirmed transaction with any input whose sequence is below 0xfffffffe, at least two below the maximum, signals that it may be replaced by a conflicting transaction paying a higher fee rate.
analogy: a tick box marked amendable on the form.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The relative timelock is the third meaning of the sequence field and the only one enforced by consensus
analogy: a gift card that activates a week after purchase
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel RelativeTimelock

meaning: Under BIP68 a version 2 input with sequence below 2 to the 31 may only be confirmed once the output it spends has aged by the sequence's value: a lock of 30 blocks allows confirmation with at least 29 blocks between the two.
analogy: a coupon valid only some days after purchase.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual Bip68Timelock; lab example

meaning: The type flag is bit 22 of the sequence, value 1 shifted left 22; set, the lock counts units of 512 seconds, clear, it counts blocks.
analogy: a switch choosing between counting turns and counting minutes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The disable flag is bit 31 of the sequence; an input with it set has no relative timelock even in a version 2 transaction, so a transaction may mix locked and unlocked inputs.
analogy: an off switch that makes the coupon valid at once.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Only the 16 least significant bits of the sequence carry the relative timelock, so the mask 0x0000ffff extracts a value of at most 65,535, which in blocks or in 512-second units is a bit more than a year.
analogy: a counter with room for only 65,535 ticks.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch reads the outputs field, the 75 bytes of Alice's transaction that assign her bitcoins to new conditions
analogy: Outputs are the lines of a till receipt: an amount and who may collect it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The output list is the outputs field as a whole: a compactSize count greater than zero, then that many outputs, each an 8-byte amount and a length-prefixed script
analogy: the change a till hands back
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel OutputList

meaning: The output count is the compactSize integer that opens the outputs field; it must be greater than zero, and Alice's transaction has two outputs.
analogy: how many envelopes of money leave the till.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The amount is the first field of an output: an 8-byte signed little-endian integer of satoshis, called value in Bitcoin Core; Alice's first output carries 20,000.
analogy: the sum on a cheque, written in the smallest coins.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin an on-chain transaction can represent; there are 100 million satoshis in a bitcoin, so 20,000 satoshis are 0.0002 bitcoin.
analogy: a cent that is a hundred-millionth of the whole note.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: The consensus range of an amount
meaning: Consensus allows an output amount from zero to 21 million bitcoins, 2.1 quadrillion satoshis; Bitcoin Core names the maximum MAX_MONEY and refuses negative, oversized and overflowing totals.
analogy: a cheque form that cannot print negative or absurd sums.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group explains the outputs that are not worth spending and the relay policy against creating them
analogy: a bank that refuses to count single cents
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel DustPolicy

meaning: An uneconomical output is one whose value is less than the extra fee that spending it would add to a transaction; a zero-value output is always uneconomical, and others become so when fee rates rise.
analogy: a coin so small the postage costs more than the coin.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin Core's dust threshold is the size of an output plus the smallest input that could spend it, times the dust relay rate of 3,000 satoshis per kilo-vbyte: 546 satoshis for a legacy P2PKH output, 294 for a P2WPKH output.
analogy: the smallest coin the post office agrees to carry.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual DustLimit; lab example

meaning: A data-carrier output is one whose script begins with OP_RETURN; it can never be spent, so nodes need not keep it, and Bitcoin Core's dust policy allows it a value of zero.
analogy: a note stuck on a parcel, carrying no money.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The output script is the last field of an output: the book says the amount is followed by a compactSize integer indicating the length of the output script, the script that contains the conditions that will need to be fulfilled in order to spend the bitcoins, and that according to consensus the minimum size of an output script is zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
analogy: the lock fitted to a new deposit box
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel OutputScriptField

meaning: The output script holds the conditions for spending an output; Alice's first is a 34-byte segwit version 1 script for Bob, her second a 22-byte segwit version 0 script for her change.
analogy: a lock fitted to the coin: whoever opens it may spend.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Consensus sets the minimum size of an output script at zero and no explicit maximum when it is created, but a later transaction can only spend an output whose script is 10,000 bytes or smaller.
analogy: a cap on how long the lock's instructions may be.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An anyone-can-spend script is one anyone can satisfy, such as the empty output script spent by an input script of OP_TRUE; upgrades take such a script and add constraints to it.
analogy: a safe left unlocked in the street.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Standard transaction outputs are the few output script templates that Bitcoin Core's policy for relaying and mining transactions allows, kept to support upgrades and to encourage putting conditions in redeem, witness and leaf scripts.
analogy: the few lock models the post office accepts.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch explains the witness structure, the 67 bytes near the end of Alice's transaction that prove she was allowed to spend
analogy: A witness is the ID you show at the counter, kept off the receipt.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: This group explains what a witness is before any byte of it is read
analogy: the ID card you show at the counter
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WitnessIdea

meaning: A witness is data that solves the math problem protecting an output, which full nodes check instead of trusting; for the script 2 OP_ADD 4 OP_EQUAL the witness is the value 2.
analogy: the answer to the riddle printed on the lock.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: Public key and signature as witness
meaning: In a digital signature scheme the public key is a public identifier of secret data and the signature a solution to an equation only the holder of that data can produce; a script of a public key and OP_CHECKSIG makes the signature the witness.
analogy: a signature only the account holder can produce.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A contract protocol is a series of transactions between parties, often signed out of order so that each party is protected before committing; the payment channel is one, and such protocols exposed the problems with witnesses in the input script.
analogy: agreements signed in advance so nobody can walk away.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group states the three problems that the book found with placing witnesses in the input script: the circular dependency, in which a refund cannot be signed before the deposit whose identifier it needs; third-party transaction malleability, in which anyone can re-encode a push in an input script and change a transaction's identifier; and second-party malleability, in which a counterparty can produce an alternative signature and change it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
analogy: re-spelling a name so the filing clerk loses the receipt
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel MalleabilityProblems

meaning: A circular dependency arises when Alice and Bob want to sign a refund before the deposit it spends, but in the legacy format the deposit's txid depends on its signatures, so the refund cannot be built until both have signed the deposit.
analogy: needing the key to get the key.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Unwanted third-party transaction malleability is a stranger's ability to change a transaction's txid without invalidating it, for example by re-encoding a push in the input script, so that a conflicting copy confirms and any transaction spending the original's outputs becomes invalid.
analogy: a stranger rewording your cheque without changing the sum.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The number 2 can be pushed as OP_2, as a one-byte push, as a two-byte push or with OP_PUSHDATA1; each is a different byte string, so each gives a legacy transaction a different txid while the script result is the same.
analogy: four ways to write the same number in words.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Unwanted second-party transaction malleability is a counterparty's ability to produce an alternative signature, because a signer chooses a random number each time, and so a conflicting transaction with a different txid that invalidates a presigned refund.
analogy: your partner re-signing a document with another pen.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Some malleability is wanted: with a signature hash the sender can allow others to change parts of a transaction, as when Bob adds an input to help pay Alice's fee; the book says unwanted when it means the other kind.
analogy: a form with a box for changes allowed by me.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Segregated witness, segwit, is the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a txid
analogy: keeping the passport photo off the ticket number
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel SegregatedWitness

meaning: Segregated witness is the separation of a transaction's witness from the data its txid is computed over; an empty input script keeps witnesses from affecting the txid and so removes circular dependencies and both unwanted malleabilities.
analogy: keeping the passport photo off the ticket number
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A hard fork is a change to the consensus rules that is not compatible with older full nodes; the obvious way to implement segwit needed one, which is why an alternative was sought.
analogy: a new road standard that old cars cannot drive on.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A soft fork is a backward-compatible change to the consensus rules: full nodes with the change must not accept any block that nodes without it would consider invalid, so new nodes can reject blocks old nodes accept but not the reverse.
analogy: a stricter road rule that old cars can still obey.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A witness program is the data in a segwit output script: a script of a number from 0 to 16 followed by 2 to 40 bytes is the segwit template, the number its version and the data the witness program; old nodes may spend it with an empty input script, new nodes require one.
analogy: a lock label saying which kind of key fits.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The witness structure is the field added by segwit to hold the data that an input script may no longer carry; it sits after the outputs and before the lock time and is not part of the txid.
analogy: an annex page stapled to the transaction.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group reads the bytes of the witness structure
analogy: annex pages bound behind the main letter
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WitnessSerialization

meaning: A witness stack is the part of the witness structure belonging to one input: a compactSize count of items followed by the items; there is one stack per input, so the structure has no count of its own.
analogy: a pile of papers handed in for one input.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A witness item is one element of a witness stack, prefixed by a compactSize integer giving its size; Alice's single item is a 65-byte signature.
analogy: one sheet in the pile, with its length stamped on.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A legacy input in a segwit transaction has a witness stack consisting entirely of a count of zero, 0x00, so the structure stays one stack per input.
analogy: an empty annex: nothing stapled to old-style inputs.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This branch covers the last field of every transaction and the first transaction of every block
analogy: A lock time is a post-dated cheque; a coinbase is the mint's wage slip.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The lock time is the four-byte field that ends every transaction
analogy: a post-dated cheque
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel LockTime

meaning: The lock time is the last 4 bytes of a transaction; zero makes it eligible for any block, and since block 31,000 a non-zero value is a consensus rule restricting which blocks may include it.
analogy: a do-not-open-before date on an envelope.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: Lock time as a block height
meaning: A lock time below 500,000,000 is a block height: the transaction can only be included in a block whose height is equal to the lock time or higher, so 123,456 allows block 123,456 and any later one.
analogy: do not open before a numbered page of the logbook.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

concept: Lock time as an epoch time
meaning: A lock time of 500,000,000 or more is an epoch time, seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00 UTC; the transaction can only be included in a block whose median time past is greater than the lock time.
analogy: do not open before this calendar date.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The median time past (MTP) of a block is the median of the timestamps of the last eleven blocks; time locks are compared with it, and it is normally an hour or two behind the clock.
analogy: asking the middle voter, not the loudest.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in each block
analogy: the mint's wage slip for the miner
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel CoinbaseTransaction

meaning: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction of a block, created by its miner to claim the block's fees and, until the subsidy runs out, newly created bitcoins; older documents call it a generation transaction.
analogy: the bonus the mint pays whoever closes the page.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A coinbase transaction's single input must have an outpoint with a null txid of all zeros and the maximal output index 0xffffffff, so that it cannot reference a previous output.
analogy: a ticket with no previous holder: printed new.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The coinbase field is the coinbase transaction's input-script field, 2 to 100 bytes long, not executed, and since BIP34 beginning with a push of the block height; it gives the transaction its name.
analogy: a free text box on the bonus slip.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The block subsidy is the newly created bitcoin a coinbase may claim: 50 BTC at first, halved every 210,000 blocks and rounded down to the satoshi, so that the total issued is just under 21 million.
analogy: a bonus that halves every four years of work.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual BlockSubsidy; lab example

meaning: The block reward is the total a miner can claim for a block, the fees of its transactions plus the subsidy; the coinbase's outputs may sum to no more than it.
analogy: the bonus plus the tips from customers.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The maturity rule says a transaction spending a coinbase output cannot be included in any block until the coinbase has 100 confirmations; outputs with fewer are called immature.
analogy: wages you cannot spend until the pay clears.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This last branch has two jobs
analogy: Weight is a transaction's postage; foundations are the post office's rules.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: Weight is the modern unit in which the size of a transaction or a block is measured, and vbytes are weight divided by four
analogy: postage that charges less for the small print
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel WeightUnits

meaning: Weight is BIP141's measure of a transaction: the legacy serialization's size times 3 plus the full serialization's size, which is 569 for Alice's transaction, the figure Bitcoin Core reports.
analogy: postage priced by volume, with signatures at a discount.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual Weight; lab example

meaning: A vbyte is a quarter of a weight unit, rounded up, so that a legacy transaction's vbytes equal its bytes; Alice's transaction is 143 vbytes.
analogy: the parcel size after the discount is applied.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Blocks are limited to 4,000,000 weight, Bitcoin Core's MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT; the header and the transaction count take a small fixed share and the rest is for transactions.
analogy: a lorry that carries four million weight units.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Each field's weight is its serialized size times a factor: 4 for the version, inputs, outputs and lock time, 1 for the marker, the flag and the witness structure; summed over Alice's transaction the factors give 569.
analogy: a price list: four for plain bytes, one for annex bytes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: This group explains the terms the chapter uses on every page without a section of its own
analogy: the foundations under a house
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Foundations

meaning: A hash function maps input of any length to a fixed-length digest, one-way and unpredictable, so that a digest can identify data and commit to it; Bitcoin's is SHA-256, with a 32-byte output.
analogy: a meat grinder: any input, a result of fixed size.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin's identifiers are double SHA-256: the hash function applied to its own output, so a txid is SHA-256 of SHA-256 of the legacy serialization, shown reversed.
analogy: running the grinder twice for safety.

meaning: The txid is the double SHA-256 of a transaction's legacy serialization, displayed in reversed byte order; for a segwit transaction it therefore excludes the witness.
analogy: a parcel's tracking number from its plain contents.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The wtxid is the double SHA-256 of the whole extended serialization, witness included; it changes when the witness changes, and blocks commit to it separately from the txid.
analogy: a tracking number that counts the annex too.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Relay policy is the set of rules a full node applies to unconfirmed transactions it relays and keeps in its memory pool; it is chosen by the node, can change, and includes dust, standardness, version 3 and replacement rules.
analogy: the house rules of one post office.

meaning: A consensus rule is a rule every full node enforces identically to decide which blocks and transactions are valid; this chapter's examples are the input and output bounds, the amount range, BIP68, the lock time, the subsidy and the maturity rule.
analogy: the law every post office must obey identically.
